# Bruce

**Independent documentation review · 2026-11-02**

A broad ESP32 firmware ecosystem with an explicit board/peripheral compatibility table.

## Documented features

| Feature | Finding | Primary source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platforms | Upstream lists Cardputer/ADV, Stick, Core and multiple LILYGO/other targets | [bruce](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pr3y/Bruce/main/README.md) |
| Installation | Official web flasher, release binaries and Launcher/M5Burner paths are documented | [bruce](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pr3y/Bruce/main/README.md) |
| Hardware dependency | The compatibility table separates built-in features and external hardware | [bruce](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pr3y/Bruce/main/README.md) |
| Custom board | Upstream documents its RF Reaper dev kit separately | [bruce](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pr3y/Bruce/main/README.md) |

## Our review

Bruce is the stronger choice when a supported handheld and a broad set of integrations reduce the amount of firmware you would otherwise write. The useful starting point is its compatibility table, not its menu. Choose the exact target first and count external modules as real parts of the system. We would prefer one well-supported board configuration over attempting to make every listed feature appear on arbitrary hardware.

## Choose it when

A maintained build explicitly covers your exact board and required peripherals.

## Skip it when

You need deep control over one custom measurement path and cannot tolerate a broad application stack.

## Compatibility and limitations

A firmware entry cannot establish a connected peripheral or verify it works. Supported functionality varies by carrier. A vendor board and an old third-party build are separate support decisions.

## Alternatives

Compare the individually reviewed Bruce, Marauder, GhostESP, HaleHound, Porkchop or Meshtastic workflows against the actual task.

## Setup and firmware route

Use the [model-appropriate installation and recovery guide](../../labs/guides/esp32-firmware.md) and the [firmware route index](../../labs/FLASHING.md). Record model/revision, current firmware, required peripherals, artifact source and digest before a write. Preserve configuration and establish the vendor recovery route first.

The [benchkit helper](../../labs/SCRIPTS.md) can record inventory, verify artifact bytes and prepare an explicit dry-run flash plan. A successful boot is only a prerequisite: verify the actual function you need.

## First evaluation

Pin source/release and board target, preserve a recovery image, and verify one benign owned-fixture task with an inspectable output before extending the system.

Keep the firmware version, fixture and failed/skipped/unobserved cases with the result. Documented ratings are not measurements performed by this project.

# M5Stack Cardputer ADV

**Independent documentation review · 2026-11-02**

A physical-keyboard embedded handheld with a model-specific input implementation.

## Documented features

| Feature | Finding | Primary source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Processor / flash | ESP32-S3FN8 at 240 MHz; 8 MB flash | [official-cardputer-adv](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer-Adv) |
| Display / keys | 1.14-inch 240×135 ST7789V2; 56 keys | [official-cardputer-adv](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer-Adv) |
| Storage / connectivity | microSD and 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi | [official-cardputer-adv](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer-Adv) |
| Audio / motion | ES8311 codec, speaker, MEMS microphone and BMI270 | [official-cardputer-adv](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer-Adv) |
| Power | 1500 mAh battery is documented | [official-cardputer-adv](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer-Adv) |
| Expansion discrepancy | Manufacturer specification lists EXT 2.54-14P plus Grove; Hydra vendor describes an 18-pin interface. Reconcile exact connector/pin map before attaching hardware. | [official-cardputer-adv](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer-Adv) |

## Our review

ADV earns consideration when the required expansion uses its documented 18-pin header or your firmware explicitly supports its revised keyboard hardware. That is a concrete compatibility benefit over the original, not a universal promise that every old binary will behave correctly. We would choose the supported host/firmware/accessory combination as a system rather than independently buying the newest names. The manufacturer’s library is direct evidence that the original and ADV are different input targets. For custom applications, that separation matters more than a generic feature list.

## Choose it when

You need a programmable pocket keyboard/display and have matched the exact target and accessories.

## Skip it when

You want to run normal Linux packages or assume original and ADV are identical hardware.

## Compatibility and limitations

The current manufacturer manual is now retrieved. Original and ADV still have distinct keyboard drivers and accessory support. On ADV, the manufacturer and Hydra accessory descriptions use inconsistent connector counts; verify the actual pin map/mechanical fit instead of silently assuming agreement. Neither is a Linux computer, and added interfaces require real documented hardware.

## Alternatives

Tab5 for touch-first interaction; Hackberry CM5 for Linux; the other Cardputer revision only when its compatibility advantage is real.

## Setup and firmware route

Use the [model-appropriate installation and recovery guide](../../labs/guides/esp32-firmware.md) and the [firmware route index](../../labs/FLASHING.md). Record model/revision, current firmware, required peripherals, artifact source and digest before a write. Preserve configuration and establish the vendor recovery route first.

The [benchkit helper](../../labs/SCRIPTS.md) can record inventory, verify artifact bytes and prepare an explicit dry-run flash plan. A successful boot is only a prerequisite: verify the actual function you need.

## First evaluation

Use the correct manufacturer library and firmware target; test modifier keys, text input and each attached peripheral before adopting an old binary.

Keep the firmware version, fixture and failed/skipped/unobserved cases with the result. Documented ratings are not measurements performed by this project.

# M5Stack Cardputer

**Independent documentation review · 2026-11-02**

A physical-keyboard embedded handheld with a model-specific input implementation.

## Documented features

| Feature | Finding | Primary source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Processor / flash | ESP32-S3FN8 at 240 MHz; 8 MB flash | [official-cardputer](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer) |
| Display / keys | 1.14-inch 240×135 ST7789V2; 56 keys | [official-cardputer](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer) |
| Storage / connectivity | microSD and 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi | [official-cardputer](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer) |
| Audio / power | I2S speaker, MEMS microphone; 120 mAh plus 1400 mAh base batteries are documented | [official-cardputer](https://docs.m5stack.com/en/core/Cardputer) |

## Our review

The original Cardputer is a useful keyboard-first embedded controller when your application fits its existing interfaces. Its physical keyboard makes local text entry much more practical than a few-button board. The most important upgrade decision is not simply whether ADV is newer: it is whether your chosen firmware supports the keyboard driver and whether the needed accessory physically matches the host. ## Choose it when

## Skip it when

The maker’s current documentation is explicit about exposed high voltage and the need for its protective shield. HackRF One is a useful first serious general-purpose SDR when wide tuning coverage, open hardware and host-side signal processing matter. It is a less convincing purchase if the requirement is simply to receive one narrow class of signals: a simpler receiver can reduce cost and complexity. The important trade is broad coverage versus 8-bit dynamic range and half-duplex operation. A higher sample-rate setting is not automatically a better measurement; it changes the bandwidth and host/storage demands.

Published range and application sensitivity need their own measurements.

A receive-only SDR for listening; a suitable higher-resolution/full-duplex SDR for those specific requirements; PortaPack for local controls.

| Antennas | Swappable LF and 13.56 MHz HF; the listed UHF add-on is not developed yet | [proxmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RfidResearchGroup/proxmark3/master/README.md) |
| Current maturity | Maintainers label firmware unstable and advise against installing the BWM add-on | [proxmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RfidResearchGroup/proxmark3/master/README.md) |

## Our review

Our recommendation is to buy for firmware development or deliberate early-adopter work, and keep a proven RDV4 available for routine bench tasks. The new MCU, FPGA and expansion connector create engineering headroom, but they do not establish that an existing workflow has already been ported and validated. The most important specification today is the maintainer support warning, not the generation number. A listing that bundles UHF or wireless expansion should not be read as proof those functions are ready.

## Choose it when

You can build, flash and debug evolving firmware and accept feature gaps.

## Skip it when

You need a stable daily RFID workflow or are buying specifically for UHF or the BWM add-on.

## Compatibility and limitations

This assessment follows the live maintainer documentation, which is actively changing. The UHF entry is a roadmap item. The wireless/battery add-on warning is separate from the presence of an ESP32-C2 in the proposed architecture. No reliability or protocol-coverage benchmark was run.

## Alternatives

Proxmark3 RDV4 for an established host-driven bench; Chameleon Ultra for a narrower emulation workflow.

uConsole is a sensible research platform if you want a modular handheld and are willing to treat the operating-system image as part of the product. Its public schematics and core-specific image table make it more inspectable than an unspecified assembled cyberdeck. We would choose a clearly documented core/image combination and resist applying upgrade instructions from another variant. The A06 power-profile tooling is an example of why ownership experience differs between cores even when the enclosure looks the same.

## Choose it when

You want a documented modular Linux handheld and can maintain its image and peripherals.

## Skip it when

You need a universal plug-and-play image across all uConsole cores or prefer conventional laptop ergonomics.

## Compatibility and limitations

The official image links include historical releases; newest is not synonymous with verified for your attached hardware. A 4G board, storage upgrade or alternative compute module has its own compatibility requirements. We did not reproduce keyboard flashing or verify a battery-runtime claim.

## Alternatives

HackberryPi CM5 for its CM5-only design; Raspberry Pi 500+ for fixed use.

# Public threat and research-persona documentation

A dossier is a set of claim/source relationships, not a verdict about a person. Public handles, organizational brands, vulnerability names, malware names, intrusion operators and government attribution labels are distinct entity types. Store a claimed alias link with its issuer and date; do not merge identities from similar handles, shared code, a hosting relationship or third-party repetition.

## Claim contract

The machine-readable ledger records claim ID, source ID, subject, narrow statement, evidence type, limitation and review date. The source registry records publisher, URL, publication date when known, retrieval date, source class and inspection status. A publication date of null is intentional. Reviewed today does not mean observed today. A government attribution statement is attributed to the agency; an organizational homepage supplies self-published claims; an incident responder supplies reported observations within its coverage.

For probability-like confidence values, use a calibrated method and labeled evaluation first. The current ledger uses categorical evidence types instead of invented numeric confidence. Reposts and summaries do not count as independent observations. Preserve contradictory claims and source-age limits.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
 S["Source receipt"] --> C["Narrow claim"]
 C --> E["Typed entity"]
 C --> U["Limits and unknowns"]
 E --> H["Competing attribution hypotheses"]
 U --> H
 H --> D["Assessment question"]
```

## Persona and intrusion separation

The Nightmare-Eclipse card concerns a public research persona. The Huntress source concerns an observed intrusion in which public tooling was used. Those statements do not identify the author as the intruder. An unsuccessful observed attempt also does not prove a tool never works. Historical patch status in a report must not be turned into current endpoint posture.

The Church of Malware card records a self-described community and public homepage bylines. The homepage alone does not independently establish nonprofit status, legal responsibility, organization membership or malicious intent. The retained handles are public bylines, not personal investigations. The ledger supplies no real names, private contacts, home addresses, account triangulation or leaked material.

## From intelligence to assessment

Translate a supported behavior-level claim into an observation requirement, a rival benign explanation and a controlled evaluation question. Example: a report of tool adoption motivates studying protection-health visibility and evidence integrity; it does not justify reproducing a security-product exploit. A help-desk-focused advisory motivates a consented identity-verification tabletop. Public intelligence supplies context, not authority to assess someone else's systems.

A future dossier must add source-version pinning, claim review expiry, corrections and independent review. These cards are an initial bounded evidence register, not a complete actor encyclopedia, a membership directory or a claim of contemporary operational intelligence coverage.

Only the observed handle and homepage association are retained; no account linkage is inferred.

## Assessment research question

Review the difference between a project description and an independently evaluated capability.

This is a proposed question, not a finding about the named entity. Use synthetic or consented fixtures under the [assessment protocol](../../assessment/PROTOCOL.md). No hosted tools were acquired or run.

[Evidence method](../METHOD.md) · [Card index](../README.md)

# Firmware installation and recovery routes

The first decision is **what artifact you have**, not which flash button to press. A factory/merged ESP image, OTA application image, UF2 file, Linux disk image and a desktop client are different things. Identify the exact board revision, firmware release, artifact kind, publisher digest and recovery route before writing hardware.

## Route index

| Route | Targets | Installation path | Recovery and verification |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FL-01 · ESP factory image | Supported S3/C5/P4 board and exact firmware target | Publisher’s official web flasher, M5Burner or a publisher-documented merged image layout | Model-specific download mode; verify target, boot log and one real function |
| FL-02 · ESP source build | A supported board configuration in the selected project | Pinned ESP-IDF/Arduino/PlatformIO environment; build before using its own flash task | Preserve original config/partition layout; recover using that board’s instructions |
| FL-03 · nRF52 UF2 | Exact Meshtastic nRF52840 target | Enter documented DFU mode and copy the matching UF2 to the bootloader volume | Confirm actual bootloader/family, then application version, region and node operation |
| FL-04 · ESP mesh BIN | ThinkNode ESP32 / correct Heltec variant | Meshtastic flasher with exact board and display selection | V4 and V4-R8 are separate; OLED/TFT images may differ |
| FL-05 · Flipper firmware | Flipper Zero | Official update tools or firmware build tool; application packages use their own API metadata | Use the upstream hardware recovery procedure; external app API major version must match |
| FL-06 · Proxmark | RDV4, PM5 or a supported generic platform | Matching host client, bootloader and firmware built for the exact platform | Run upstream client/device validation; PM5 is currently described as unstable |
| FL-07 · Chameleon | Ultra, Lite or Devkit | Current upstream client/GUI and exact device firmware instructions | Confirm model, firmware/client pair and supported reader/emulation mode |
| FL-08 · Linux disk image | Exact uConsole core, CM5 carrier or Pi computer | Verify the official image; write only to the explicitly identified removable target | Preserve a known-good removable image and configuration; test fresh boot and restoration |
| FL-09 · HackRF / PortaPack | Base SDR plus exact add-on | Matched vendor/upstream host, device and Mayhem release instructions | Identify both boards; do not substitute seller-custom images for another revision |

## Build examples supported by the retrieved sources

These are preparation/build steps, not a claim that hardware was flashed in this environment.

### Flipper application/firmware development

```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/flipperdevices/flipperzero-firmware.git
cd flipperzero-firmware
./fbt
```

Pin a release/commit for reproducibility before the build. Use `./fbt build APPSRC=applications_user/your_app` for an application you wrote. FAPs are ELF-based application packages with metadata; they are copied into RAM and checked against the exported API. See [the Flipper walkthrough](guides/flipper-development.md).

### Tab5 official demo

The [official demo](https://github.com/m5stack/M5Tab5-UserDemo) documents dependency retrieval and ESP-IDF v5.4.2:

```bash
python fetch_repos.py
cd platforms/tab5
idf.py build
```

Run inside a pinned checkout with the documented SDK initialized. Its desktop build is a separate SDL/CMake route; a successful desktop UI does not validate the physical display, camera or radio coprocessor.

### Monstatek M1

The [current source](https://github.com/Monstatek/M1) documents `./build.sh --release`, CMake, Ninja, Arm GCC 14.2 and `srec_cat`, with a clean working tree required for release artifacts. Use its hardware-revision documentation. An STM32 artifact is not an ESP32 image and must not be given to an ESP installer.

## Use benchkit before a write

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit inventory
python -m labtools.benchkit verify path/to/official.bin --sha256 PUBLISHER_SHA256
python -m labtools.benchkit flash-plan path/to/manifest.json --board cardputer-adv --port /dev/ttyACM0
```

Replace `PUBLISHER_SHA256` with the independently obtained publisher digest. A matching digest identifies bytes; it does not authenticate a source by itself. A manifest needs `board`, `chip`, `kind`, `offset`, `file`, `sha256` and `source_url`. The helper only plans an explicitly declared merged factory `.bin` at `0x0` for one of its supported profiles. It **never executes** the generated argument list, erases flash, writes a serial port or chooses a disk. OTA/app-only images must use their own documented route. A declaration in your manifest is not proof that a binary is valid for the board.

The repository’s `example.bin` is synthetic text, not firmware. Its example-only manifest is intentionally rejected by `flash-plan`. This gives a repeatable failure case without writing hardware.

## After installation

1. Read and record the version and board target from a reliable device/client view.
2. Verify display, input and storage before testing attached peripherals.
3. Restore only configuration compatible with the current firmware and partition scheme.
4. Use an owned fixture for one expected function and one negative case.
5. Keep the artifact digest, config backup, output and recovery notes together.

## Primary references

- [Espressif esptool commands](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esptool/en/latest/esp32s3/esptool/basic-commands.html)
- [UF2 format specification](https://github.com/microsoft/uf2)
- [Flipper build and external applications](https://github.com/flipperdevices/flipperzero-firmware/tree/dev/documentation)
- [Meshtastic model-specific hardware documentation](https://github.com/meshtastic/meshtastic/tree/master/docs/hardware/devices)
- [RRG Proxmark client/platform documentation](https://github.com/RfidResearchGroup/proxmark3)
- [Research source receipts](../hardware/PRIMARY-SOURCES.md)

# NIGHTSHIFT practical workbench

Use the tools to answer a concrete engineering question. Each walkthrough names the required inputs, commands, expected result, failure cases and evidence to retain. Offline fixtures are deliberately synthetic; hardware steps are marked as requiring a device.

## Start with runnable local examples

From the repository root with Python 3.12:

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit inventory
python -m labtools.benchkit telemetry labs/fixtures/messages.csv
python -m labtools.benchkit ble-decode 02010605094c414231
python -m labtools.benchkit pincheck labs/fixtures/pins-good.json
python -m labtools.benchkit power --capacity-mah 1200 --active-ma 80 --idle-ma 5 --duty 0.1
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

Expected highlights: eight of ten synthetic messages were observed; median latency is 60 ms. The advertisement decodes a flags structure and the fictional local name `LAB1`. The pin fixture has three unique pins and one explicitly shared signal. The power calculation gives 12.5 mA average and a 76.8-hour planning estimate under its stated assumptions—not a device battery-life result.

## Walkthroughs

| Track | Full walkthrough | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Embedded software | [ESP32 firmware](guides/esp32-firmware.md) | Identify target, artifact type, installer and recovery route |
| Mesh communication | [LoRa node](guides/mesh-node.md) | Separate hardware role, region, firmware target, delivery and power |
| Portable applications | [Flipper development](guides/flipper-development.md) | Build an application and understand API/RAM constraints |
| RFID | [RFID bench](guides/rfid-bench.md) | Choose reader/emulator and a versioned reference fixture |
| Linux devices | [Cyberdeck setup](guides/linux-cyberdeck.md) | Preserve an image, validate the complete host and keep a recovery path |
| RF signals | [SDR bench](guides/sdr-bench.md) | Set an input budget and inspect a controlled receive path |
| Network/application evidence | [Local network lab](guides/local-network.md) | Distinguish HTTP response, transport error and passive observation |
| Detection and forensics | [Evidence lab](guides/evidence-analysis.md) | Write a harmless detection rule, inspect a toy binary and preserve evidence |
| Engineering assurance | [Assurance and recovery](guides/assurance.md) | Model states, validate configuration and test restoration |

See [firmware routes and recovery](FLASHING.md), [helper script reference](SCRIPTS.md), and [the lab index](CATALOG.md) for the individual exercises. Use [the product documentation](../site/reviews.html) to choose equipment; a method that works on one model is not automatically valid on another.

## What has actually been tested

The Python helper tests exercise hashes, manifest/board mismatch, example-only artifact refusal, pin collisions, malformed BLE structures, UF2 structure, timing errors, loopback-only requests and power assumptions. The browser suite tests site interactions. These are software tests of this repository. Physical flashes, RF trials, instrument calibration and device-specific endurance remain hardware exercises and are not reported as passed.

# Benchkit: custom engineering helpers

All commands run from the repository root with Python 3.12 and its standard library. Source: [`labtools/benchkit.py`](../labtools/benchkit.py). Outputs are JSON; a detected invalid input returns exit status 1 and an explanation on stderr. Use shell redirection to retain a report, for example `python -m labtools.benchkit telemetry labs/fixtures/messages.csv > /tmp/message-report.json`.

| Command | Input | What it checks / produces | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `inventory` | None | Python/platform and candidate serial device paths | Opens no device; identifies no board automatically |
| `verify FILE --sha256 HEX` | Artifact and expected digest | Streamed SHA-256 comparison and byte count | Integrity check, not publisher authentication |
| `flash-plan MANIFEST --board PROFILE --port PORT` | Explicit manifest/profile/port | Dry-run esptool argument list after board/chip/type/digest checks | Never executes; only declared merged factory ESP images |
| `uf2-inspect FILE` | UF2 bytes | Block magic, block sequence, family identifiers and address summary | Not a signature, bootability or compatibility verdict |
| `telemetry FILE` | Message CSV | Sent, observed, missing, delivery fraction and observed latency | Assumes synchronized fixture timestamps |
| `ble-decode HEX` | An offline BLE advertisement | Length/type/value structures and local-name text | No radio operations or device identity inference |
| `pincheck FILE` | JSON pin/signal records | Conflicting net assignments and explicitly shared signals | Not an electrical or voltage check |
| `http URL` | Loopback HTTP(S) URL | Status, content type, byte count and body digest | Rejects external targets and redirects to them |
| `power --capacity-mah N --active-ma N --idle-ma N --duty F` | Consistent battery-side current assumptions | Weighted average current and estimated hours | Planning calculation, not a product test |

## Firmware manifest

```json
{
  "board": "cardputer-adv",
  "chip": "esp32s3",
  "kind": "merged-factory",
  "offset": "0x0",
  "file": "official-release.bin",
  "sha256": "REPLACE_WITH_64_HEX_PUBLISHER_DIGEST",
  "source_url": "https://github.com/pr3y/Bruce/releases"
}
```

The artifact path is relative to the manifest. Use the schema only if the publisher actually identifies the artifact and layout this way. Supported profiles are in [board-profiles.json](fixtures/board-profiles.json). The standard Cardputer and ADV are separate profiles even though both use S3. Tab5’s application processor is P4; its radio coprocessor is not the same flash target. This example is a template and is not valid until real metadata is supplied.

## Reproduce successful and failed cases

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit telemetry labs/fixtures/messages.csv
python -m labtools.benchkit pincheck labs/fixtures/pins-good.json
python -m labtools.benchkit pincheck labs/fixtures/pins-conflict.json
python -m labtools.benchkit ble-decode 02010605094c414231
python -m labtools.benchkit ble-decode 0509ff
```

The third and fifth commands must fail. A test that treats their nonzero exit as success would hide the error being demonstrated. A missing receive time stays missing; it is not silently replaced with zero latency. A pin may be shared only when both records declare the same signal name.

## Scope and extension

The helpers inspect inputs and prepare records; they do not scan public networks, transmit RF, clone credentials, install firmware or launch third-party payloads. Add a new board profile only after checking its chip and publisher installation format. Extend tests alongside any parser or validation change. See [the walkthrough index](README.md) for when to use each helper and [the tests](../tests/test_benchkit.py) for executable edge cases.

# Assurance and recovery: test the failure path

**Outcome:** a configuration record, a small state model and an executed recovery result.

## 1. State what must remain true

For a firmware-update workflow, define states such as `known_good`, `downloaded`, `verified`, `staged`, `booted` and `recovered`. State invariants before writing code: an unverified artifact cannot be staged; the recovery path must not depend only on the image being replaced; a successful boot must still be followed by a functional check.

Use the [firmware helper](../SCRIPTS.md) as a small example: it rejects a board/chip mismatch, unsupported artifact layout and example-only fixture before producing a dry-run plan. Those checks do not prove every state transition of a physical bootloader.

## 2. Validate the configuration graph

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit pincheck labs/fixtures/pins-good.json
python -m labtools.benchkit pincheck labs/fixtures/pins-conflict.json
```

The first input deliberately shares one SPI clock net. The second assigns two different chip-select signals to the same pin and must fail. This is a graph/net-name check, not a validation of voltage, current, pull-ups, timing or bus arbitration. Extend the design review with the actual schematic and source manual.

## 3. Separate requirement from observation

Build a compatibility table with explicit statuses: documented, locally software-tested, physically tested, failed and unknown. Include exact versions and conditions. Do not promote “the parser accepts the record” into “the hardware works,” or “the container starts” into “the service is ready.”

## 4. Exercise a reversible restoration

For a local learning service, create a small owned configuration and a known-good copy, change a noncritical setting, restore it and make the same functional request again. Keep the before/after digest and observed response. For a Linux device, boot the recovery medium independently. For a microcontroller, use only its documented download/recovery path and a noncritical fixture.

## 5. Design negative tests

Try a wrong board target, mismatched checksum, truncated UF2, malformed BLE length, duplicate message sequence and receive-before-send timestamp. The expected outcome is a specific refusal or error, with no silent fallback. The [benchkit tests](../../tests/test_benchkit.py) implement these software cases; hardware recovery is separately recorded.

## 6. Connect the result to system engineering

Use the [formal assurance domain](../../atlas/02-formal-software-assurance.md) for invariant thinking, [supply-chain provenance](../../atlas/04-supply-chain-and-provenance.md) for artifact identity, [cloud systems](../../atlas/08-cloud-systems.md) for service readiness and [response/resilience](../../atlas/13-response-resilience.md) for restoration. These share a method: define a falsifier, preserve evidence and test the path that matters when the normal path fails.

# ESP32 firmware: identify, build, recover

**Outcome:** a repeatable installation record for an exact board and firmware release. Hardware writing is a device exercise; the local preparation checks can run without a board.

## 1. Define the whole target

Write down the board/model/revision, MCU, display controller, keyboard/input hardware, flash/PSRAM, peripherals, power arrangement and desired firmware release. A Cardputer and Cardputer ADV both use ESP32-S3, but the manufacturer library selects different keyboard readers. Heltec V4 and V4-R8 have distinct images and pinouts. Tab5 splits application processing on P4 from wireless on C6. A chip-family match alone is insufficient.

## 2. Identify the artifact

Use the publisher release or official flasher. Record whether it is a merged factory image, app-only/OTA binary, filesystem image or source build. Record the independent digest and install layout. Do not guess flash offsets from a filename. The [route index](../FLASHING.md) explains the distinctions.

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit inventory
python -m labtools.benchkit verify path/to/download.bin --sha256 PUBLISHER_SHA256
```

A mismatch is a stopping result for that artifact, not an invitation to replace the expected digest with the observed one. A candidate `/dev/ttyACM0` path does not prove the board model.

## 3. Choose a supported development route

- Arduino/PlatformIO: use the project’s board environment and pinned library versions, not a generic target selected by appearance.
- ESP-IDF: initialize the documented SDK version and build the checked-out project in its documented directory.
- Official web flasher/M5Burner: choose the exact target and read the artifact/release notes.

For a simple application you own, begin with serial output, one button and a static display. Add storage, radio and external modules separately. Keep each known-good stage recoverable.

## 4. Plan before writing

The [benchkit manifest](../SCRIPTS.md) can bind an artifact to an explicit board/chip and produce a dry-run argument list. It does not discover or authenticate hardware and never executes writes. The example-only fixture deliberately refuses to create a hardware-write plan:

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit flash-plan labs/fixtures/example-manifest.json --board cardputer --port /dev/ttyACM0
```

Expected: exit 1, explaining that example fixtures cannot produce a board-write plan.

## 5. Recovery is model-specific

Use the vendor’s download-mode sequence and recovery artifact. StickS3’s current manual describes holding its side reset button until the internal green LED flashes. PaperS3 describes its own power-button/red-light sequence. Those instructions must not be generalized to every ESP32 enclosure. Preserve configuration and the previous partition layout before changing firmware managers.

## 6. Demonstrate readiness

Record boot/version output, correct display and key operation, storage access and one desired peripheral function. For an attached radio/NFC module, record the actual component and configured pins. A menu entry is not a detected peripheral. Compare an expected result with a negative fixture case, then test the documented recovery route.

**Sources:** [Espressif esptool](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/esptool/en/latest/esp32s3/esptool/basic-commands.html), [M5Stack manuals](https://docs.m5stack.com/), [manufacturer Cardputer keyboard implementation](https://github.com/m5stack/M5Cardputer/blob/master/src/utility/Keyboard/Keyboard.cpp), and [the primary-source ledger](../../hardware/PRIMARY-SOURCES.md).

# Evidence lab: hashes, a harmless rule and a toy binary

**Outcome:** a small inspectable chain from source input to tool output. All example data is fictional or authored in this repository.

## 1. Preserve original bytes

Use a copy of a harmless fixture. Record source path, acquisition time, byte count and SHA-256 before analysis. For artifacts with a publisher digest, compare against that independently obtained value rather than copying the newly calculated hash into the expected field.

```bash
openssl dgst -sha256 labs/fixtures/example.bin
```

OpenSSL is optional; the standard-library verification helper can do the digest comparison. A hash match establishes byte equality to the expected digest, not who authored the bytes or whether an executable is safe.

## 2. Write an explainable YARA rule

The [original classroom rule](../../examples/yara/nightshift.yar) matches a marker deliberately placed in [training.txt](../../examples/yara/training.txt). If the YARA CLI is installed:

```bash
yara examples/yara/nightshift.yar examples/yara/training.txt
yara examples/yara/nightshift.yar labs/fixtures/health.json
```

Expected: the marker rule matches the first file and does not match the second. A rule condition holding is the entire conclusion; it does not identify malware. Try moving the marker beyond the rule’s file-size limit and explain why the outcome changes. See the [official rule syntax](https://yara.readthedocs.io/en/stable/writingrules.html).

## 3. Compile a binary whose source you know

With a C compiler installed:

```bash
cc -O0 -g examples/benign_counter.c -o /tmp/nightshift-counter
/tmp/nightshift-counter
```

Expected output: `observed=3`. Inspect this binary in Ghidra: identify `main`, the loop and the constant limit, then compare disassembly/decompilation with the source. Optimize a second build and explain why the representation changes without changing the expected output. Decompiled text is a reconstruction, not the original C source. No unknown binary is downloaded or run.

## 4. Read offline protocol structures

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit ble-decode 02010605094c414231
```

The fictional advertisement decodes Flags and the local name `LAB1`. A malformed length must be rejected. A name or manufacturer-data field is an observation, not proof of a device vendor, operator, surveillance function or physical location.

## 5. Hand off a bounded conclusion

Include input digests, source/program version, command, relevant output, interpretation and limits. Label synthetic fixtures. Keep facts separate from inferred identity. Record failed and negative cases. An evidence handoff should let another person repeat the analysis without needing your shell history or unrelated private records.

**References:** [YARA rules](https://yara.readthedocs.io/en/stable/writingrules.html), [OpenSSL digests](https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-dgst/), [Ghidra](https://github.com/NationalSecurityAgency/ghidra), [forensic evidence research](../../atlas/06-forensic-science.md).

# Flipper: write a small application and understand its limits

**Outcome:** a buildable application structure, a pinned SDK/API record and a documented recovery path. The example logs a message; it does not use radios or credentials.

## 1. Establish the official development checkout

Follow the [official firmware requirements](https://github.com/flipperdevices/flipperzero-firmware). Clone with submodules and pin the release/commit used for your device. Use the repository’s build tool rather than assembling an unrelated compiler environment.

```bash
git clone --recursive https://github.com/flipperdevices/flipperzero-firmware.git
cd flipperzero-firmware
./fbt
```

## 2. Add an application you own

Copy this repository’s [example](../../examples/flipper_hello/nightshift_hello.c) and [manifest](../../examples/flipper_hello/application.fam) into `applications_user/nightshift_hello` in that official checkout. The manifest identifies the external application and entry point; the C file logs a harmless startup line and returns.

```bash
./fbt build APPSRC=applications_user/nightshift_hello
```

Expected: the pinned SDK produces a FAP application artifact or reports a specific manifest/API/build error. This repository has not compiled that example against every firmware SDK; build/launch on a physical Flipper is a hardware-track check, not a claimed local test pass.

## 3. Know what a FAP is

The [upstream application documentation](https://github.com/flipperdevices/flipperzero-firmware/blob/dev/documentation/AppsOnSDCard.md) describes FAPs as ELF-based executables with metadata/resources. The loader checks compatibility, copies code/data into RAM and relocates imported symbols. Consequently:

- SD capacity is not application runtime memory.
- External code/data consumes heap that a built-in application would use differently.
- Compatibility follows exported API metadata, including a major-version check; a filename alone does not prove compatibility.
- Debug/release firmware and application builds need to match the debugging setup.

## 4. Run only after the build is understood

Use the official tool’s documented deployment/launch route and your owned device. Retain the firmware revision, API version and application artifact digest. Verify the logged message through the documented debug/serial path. Do not describe a successful compile as proof of physical peripheral behavior.

## 5. Extend one feature at a time

Add a display view, then button handling, then a local data file before considering an external interface. Name the input and expected output for each step. Keep the original example as a recovery/build reference and follow the official firmware recovery instructions if an update fails.

**Continue:** [Flipper review](../../hardware/reviews/flipper-zero.md), [flashing routes](../FLASHING.md), and [benchkit verification](../SCRIPTS.md).

# Linux cyberdeck: make the image and peripherals reproducible

**Outcome:** a recoverable Linux workspace on an exact compute-module/carrier combination.

## 1. Inventory the complete machine

Write down compute module, RAM, carrier, display, keyboard, storage, power, cooling and optional radios. HackberryPi CM5 is documented as CM5-only and normally excludes the compute module. uConsole publishes separate CM4/A06/R01 images. A shared enclosure name does not imply one OS image fits all cores.

## 2. Verify image provenance and target storage

Use the exact vendor or maintained distribution image and its independent checksum/signature instructions. Keep a second known-good removable image. Identify the intended storage device through the operating system’s disk inventory before using a writer; this guide deliberately supplies no guessed destructive disk command.

Use `benchkit verify` for a publisher-provided SHA-256. An old source offering only MD5 is not equivalent to a modern authenticated release path; consult current distribution guidance rather than treating any matching hash as authenticity.

## 3. Validate before customizing

On first boot, record OS/kernel versions, storage identity and peripheral behavior. Check keyboard/modifiers, display orientation, charging, suspend/resume and storage access. Then run one local task you care about: edit a small file, run a unit suite or serve the local fixture.

```bash
python -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory labs/fixtures
```

In another terminal:

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit http http://127.0.0.1:8765/health.json
```

Expected: HTTP 200 and a content/body receipt. Stop the server when done.

## 4. Add one integration at a time

Add an SSD, GNSS, SDR, NFC or external Wi-Fi adapter only after the base image is recorded. Check bus/power conflicts and driver support. A port physically accepting an adapter is not evidence of supported functionality. Hackberry’s maker documents metal-case/antenna considerations; uConsole’s image/core differences affect power and kernel support.

## 5. Test recovery and ownership cost

Reboot from the known-good medium and confirm you can restore configuration without relying on the experimental storage. Record dependency versions and the complete bill of materials. For Armbian, inspect the exact board support status: standard, community-maintained, work in progress and end of life are distinct.

**Sources:** [ClockworkPi uConsole](https://github.com/clockworkpi/uConsole), [HackberryPi CM5](https://github.com/ZitaoTech/HackberryPiCM5), [Armbian build framework](https://github.com/armbian/build), and [product reviews](../../site/reviews.html).

# Local network lab: response, transport and interpretation

**Outcome:** a repeatable HTTP observation and a clear distinction between server behavior and connection failure.

## 1. Start your own harmless fixture

From the repository root:

```bash
python -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory labs/fixtures
```

Use a second terminal for requests. Keep the first terminal visible so the request can be paired with its server log.

## 2. Compare success and a real HTTP error

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit http http://127.0.0.1:8765/health.json
python -m labtools.benchkit http http://127.0.0.1:8765/not-present.txt
curl --noproxy '*' --include http://127.0.0.1:8765/health.json
curl --noproxy '*' --fail http://127.0.0.1:8765/not-present.txt
```

The helper records status, content type, byte count and body digest without dumping arbitrary headers. Expect HTTP 200 for the fixture and HTTP 404 for the missing file. The latter still proves that an HTTP server answered; curl’s `--fail` makes it return exit 22. The helper reports `http_success: false` for 404 while successfully recording the observation.

## 3. Compare a transport failure

Stop only the server you started, then repeat the first request. A connection error is different from a 404 response. Record the underlying exit status rather than hiding it behind a successful pipe or a shell message.

## 4. Add browser/proxy observation

Use browser developer tools or configure Burp/ZAP for a disposable browser profile and this local fixture. Observe one request and response with active scanning/interception disabled. Explain method, path, status and content type. A passive scan alert is a rule finding, not proof of exploitation. Do not mix unrelated browsing or personal session data into the record.

## 5. Packet evidence is a separate layer

If Wireshark/TShark is installed, use a harmless saved capture from a classroom fixture. A display filter changes the view of existing packets; it does not recover absent traffic. Identify packet bytes that support a decoded field and distinguish them from capture metadata. Do not make collecting live third-party traffic a prerequisite for this lab.

The custom helper is deliberately loopback-only and also rejects redirects to external destinations. Tests exercise that boundary as well as HTTP 200/404 behavior.

**References:** [curl manual](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html), [TShark manual](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/man-pages/tshark.html), [ZAP passive scanning](https://www.zaproxy.org/docs/desktop/start/features/pscan/), and [the core tool guide](../../foundations/TOOLS.md).

# LoRa mesh: choose the role, measure the result

**Outcome:** an exact firmware target, a role-appropriate node and an interpretable delivery/power record. No claimed radio range is inferred from an enclosure or video.

## 1. Pick a deployment role

| Need | Concrete candidates | Why it changes the design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carried tracker | ThinkNode M3, Heltec T1 | Size, charging, GNSS and enclosure matter |
| Text entry without a phone | ThinkNode M9 | Keyboard and larger display are real input features |
| Indoor fixed gateway | ThinkNode M7 | Ethernet/PoE, not a handheld battery package |
| Outdoor solar | SenseCAP P1/P1 Pro, ThinkNode M6 | Mounting, energy balance and maintenance dominate |
| Sensor development | Wio L1, Heltec V4 variants | Exposed buses and recovery are useful |

## 2. Bind hardware, region and image

Match the regional RF hardware to the legal configuration for the installation. Confirm the antenna band. Then select the exact firmware target. nRF52840 nodes commonly use UF2; ESP32 nodes use different binary/flasher paths. M1 and M5 are not interchangeable because they have similarly sized e-paper screens. V4-R8 is not original V4; its OLED/TFT targets are separate. Wio L1 e-paper also has its own image.

## 3. Establish a controlled pair

Use two owned nodes, a recorded firmware/configuration pair, a fixed initial placement and a small numbered-message sequence. Record sent time, observed receive time, missing messages, resets, power source and GNSS availability. Do not substitute phone position for a board GNSS observation without labeling it.

```csv
sequence,sent_ms,received_ms
1,0,50
2,100,170
3,200,
```

Use synchronized timestamps if computing one-way latency. Otherwise report round-trip observations or clock uncertainty instead.

## 4. Analyze the provided synthetic example

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit telemetry labs/fixtures/messages.csv
```

Expected: 10 sent, 8 observed, 2 missing, delivery fraction 0.8 and median observed latency 60 ms. These are arithmetic fixture results, not measured Meshtastic performance. Missing messages have no invented latency.

## 5. Budget energy separately

```bash
python -m labtools.benchkit power --capacity-mah 1200 --active-ma 80 --idle-ma 5 --duty 0.1 --usable 0.8
```

Expected planning estimate: 12.5 mA average and 76.8 hours. Use battery-side currents at a consistent voltage; include conversion loss and actual GNSS/display workload in a real design. A solar panel rating is not daily energy and cell capacity is not measured winter autonomy.

## 6. Repeat and retain failures

Only after the stationary baseline should you change one variable: placement, obstruction, antenna, firmware or workload. Keep the negative cases and topology with the result. Track configuration recovery, not just a successful first message. For outdoor nodes, include maintenance access and charge/brownout logs over representative conditions.

**Sources:** [Meshtastic hardware manuals](https://github.com/meshtastic/meshtastic/tree/master/docs/hardware/devices), the individually reviewed [product library](../../site/reviews.html), and [source receipts](../../hardware/PRIMARY-SOURCES.md).

# RFID bench: separate a reader, emulator and evidence trail

**Outcome:** a model/client/firmware matrix and an owned reference fixture. This is an engineering workflow, not a credential-copying procedure.

## 1. Choose the instrument for the question

Use a host-driven Proxmark workflow when the result needs detailed client-side records and analysis. Consider Chameleon for a defined supported emulation task. Ultra and Devkit include the documented MFRC522 HF reader hardware; Lite does not. The Chameleon whitepaper separates hardware capability, firmware support and implemented application behavior—those columns must not be collapsed into one “supported” label.

Proxmark5 is also not an automatic production-ready upgrade. The currently retrieved maintainer README describes its firmware as unstable, warns against its BWM add-on and identifies UHF as not developed. Use the exact present release notes when making a purchase or migration decision.

## 2. Record compatibility before connecting a fixture

Create an inventory containing model/revision, antenna, host OS, client build, bootloader/firmware, documented tag mode and expected observation. Keep the reference tag and reader owned and labeled. A decoded identifier is not an identity or authorization conclusion.

| Check | Expected evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Physical model | Board/label and source manual agree |
| Host/device versions | Matching supported client/firmware record |
| Mode support | Current implemented mode, not only potential silicon support |
| Reference fixture | Known type, ownership, orientation and distance |
| Repeatability | Repeated observations and explicitly failed cases |

## 3. Prepare software using upstream validation

Use the RRG platform-specific compilation and client-validation documentation. Generic PM3 builds and RDV4 are not the same target. Some generic boards have 256 KB flash and require reduced builds; do not project that warning onto every PM3. For Chameleon, choose a currently maintained client and its supported firmware route.

## 4. Make the first experiment modest

Confirm that the client identifies the device and correctly classifies a known owned reference tag. Repeat under fixed conditions and retain negative observations. Change only one thing—client version, antenna position or fixture—before repeating. If investigating emulation, use an owned development reader and a fictional fixture dataset rather than a live access credential.

## 5. Preserve provenance

Hash the exported non-sensitive logs and keep a fixture description, device versions and conditions with them. Do not treat an emulated response as proof of general reader compatibility or a vulnerability. Define what would falsify the interpretation before expanding the test.

**Sources:** [RRG Proxmark](https://github.com/RfidResearchGroup/proxmark3), [Chameleon hardware](https://github.com/RfidResearchGroup/ChameleonUltra/wiki/hardware), [Chameleon technical whitepaper](https://github.com/RfidResearchGroup/ChameleonUltra/wiki/technical_whitepaper), and [individual reviews](../../site/reviews.html).

# SDR bench: a controlled signal before a sweeping claim

**Outcome:** a documented receive path and an interpretable sample record.

## 1. Define the measurement

Choose one known reference signal, receiver configuration and expected observation. Write down frequency, modulation, sample rate, gain, antenna/cabled path, attenuation and recording duration. For a synthetic or shielded bench exercise, use a known signal source or previously recorded harmless samples rather than unrelated live traffic.

## 2. Respect the actual instrument architecture

HackRF One is documented as a 1 MHz–6 GHz half-duplex SDR with 8-bit conversion and 2–20 Msps quadrature sample rates. It cannot transmit and receive simultaneously as a full-duplex device. PortaPack changes the operating interface; it does not remove the base radio’s conversion limits. Seller-specific SDR/PortaPack bundles need exact compatibility verification.

## 3. Budget the input before connecting

The HackRF One manual specifies a maximum input of −5 dBm. A direct source connection requires a properly calculated attenuation/protection path, not an assumption that low software gain protects the front end. Record source level, attenuation, cable loss and uncertainty. A nearby strong source can also overload the receive path.

## 4. Record a small baseline

Begin receive-only with a known controlled input. Keep the original sample bytes and settings. Check for clipping and expected bandwidth before interpreting a spectrum image. Estimate storage before capture: complex I/Q with signed 8-bit I and Q uses approximately `2 × sample_rate × seconds` bytes, excluding metadata. At 2 Msps for 10 seconds that is about 40 MB.

## 5. Compare one variable

Change sample rate, gain or antenna position one at a time. A wider display is not automatically higher resolution or sensitivity. Keep signal-processing settings and software versions with the recording. Do not turn uncalibrated amplitude into a power measurement or an image peak into a device identity.

## 6. Decide whether this is the right tool

Choose a simpler receive-only SDR for a narrow listening requirement, a higher-resolution/full-duplex instrument if those are hard requirements, or a calibrated analyzer when amplitude accuracy is the task. General coverage is useful, but it is not a substitute for specifying the measurement.

**Sources:** [HackRF One hardware documentation](https://github.com/greatscottgadgets/hackrf/blob/master/docs/source/hackrf_one.rst), [Mayhem compatibility guidance](https://github.com/portapack-mayhem/mayhem-firmware), and [the SDR reviews](../../site/reviews.html).

## Thesis contribution test

A thesis contribution must be narrower than a platform name: a new identifiable model, a validated uncertainty method, an experimentally supported mechanism, a counterexample that changes an engineering decision, or a reproducible negative finding. Distinguish implementation effort from scientific novelty. Compare with original research in the chosen specialty before claiming novelty; this extension provides a research agenda, not an exhaustive literature review.

For examination, score correctness of derivation, relevance of the comparator, provenance, independence of the test partition, quality of uncertainty analysis, resource realism and clarity of the falsifier. Independent examiner review and scored results remain pending.

# Reference experiments and measured limits

These six offline experiments use Python's standard library. They exercise bounded mechanics; they are neither completed HELIOS missions nor evidence of deployed defense effectiveness. Synthetic outputs, seed, schema, assumptions and hashes are retained under [data/synthetic](../data/synthetic). The seventh figure derives from the issuer-maintained CISA metadata snapshot.

```bash
python -m experiments.benchmark
python scripts/build_research_visuals.py
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
```

## KEPLER Nightwatch · detector evaluation

![Synthetic detector trace with a frozen decision threshold](assets/telemetry.svg)

6,000 synthetic samples at 30-second intervals use correlated noise, declared anomaly intervals, two missing blocks and a benign test-period mean shift. Training covers samples 0–2999, validation 3000–4499 and test 4500–5999. Mean/std and median/MAD scores use training parameters; the 99.75th percentile threshold uses labeled benign validation samples. This calibration is supervised, not unsupervised.

The test contains 1,440 observed samples and 80 labeled anomalous samples. Both methods produce 80 true positives and 127 false positives: precision 0.386, timestamp recall 1.0 and 10.58 false alerts per observed hour. They have identical decisions because both scores are monotone affine transformations and use the same percentile criterion. This comparison cannot demonstrate an advantage from robust normalization. All three synthetic events are detected at their first available sample. These outcomes depend on deliberately strong injected anomalies and say nothing about real incident detection.

The 200-replicate, 50-row block-bootstrap precision interval is approximately [0.000, 0.618]. Zero can occur when sampled blocks include no anomalies but do include false alerts. This is a finite-fixture diagnostic with only three test events, not a credible universal performance guarantee. The drift challenge, missingness, event scoring and false-alert denominator matter more than claiming success from high recall.

## PHOENIX Relay · constrained recovery scheduling

![Weighted service loss for three recovery orders](assets/recovery.svg)

Enumerating six synthetic repair jobs yields 25 prerequisite-feasible schedules. The mission-weight greedy baseline loses 10.60 weighted service-minutes; shortest-ready-first and exhaustive optimization both lose 9.64. The optimum is exact only for this six-job, deterministic, single-crew objective. No claim is made about multi-crew, uncertain-duration or real incident recovery. Extend the model with common repair dependencies and held-out duration scenarios before drawing operational conclusions.

## ORION Lifeboat · update interruption boundaries

![Four interruption cases compared across abstract update strategies](assets/firmware.svg)

The two-slot model can select a verified image at all four complete-operation interruption boundaries; a single-slot model can do so in two. This result assumes atomic individual operations, reliable verification and slot availability. The code does not implement secure boot, signature verification, torn-write handling, flash emulation or protection against simultaneous storage failure. Those are falsification tasks for the graduate mission rather than hidden claims of the reference model.

## EUROPA Clock · partial temporal order

![Uncertainty intervals for three synthetic observers](assets/clocks.svg)

Naively sorting two observer timestamps puts sensor before gateway, while fixture truth has gateway first. Their uncertainty intervals overlap, so the interval model returns indeterminate. Both intervals precede archive. Closed intervals that merely touch remain indeterminate. Bounds are assumed and contain the fixture truth; the reference cannot estimate unknown clock bias or establish causation.

## LUNAR Veil · privacy and utility relation

![Analytic Laplace count-error curve](assets/privacy.svg)

For a unit-bounded count query, Laplace expected absolute error equals sensitivity/epsilon. Twelve sequential releases have a basic composed budget of 12 epsilon. This analytic curve implements no data-release mechanism, protected data ingestion, clipping, secure randomness or production privacy accountant. A future experiment must define the protected entity and contribution limit before invoking a privacy guarantee. See [NIST SP 800-226](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/226/final).

## LUNAR GATEWAY Courier · contact-limited evidence

![Synthetic age of information across contact windows](assets/contacts.svg)

A four-hour fixture assumes an eight-minute contact in each hour, with ideal verified delivery at every connected sample. It produces 32 contact-only attempts versus 240 always-attempt steps, with maximum information age 52 minutes. Attempts are an energy proxy, not joules. Queue capacity, signature checks, stale receipts, packet loss and real spacecraft contacts remain unimplemented.

## NEOWISE Chronicle · real metadata, narrow interpretation

![Monthly additions from the pinned CISA catalog snapshot](assets/kev.svg)

The [snapshot](../data/research/kev_snapshot.json) retains 1,731 KEV entries from catalog release 2026-10-01. Five public metadata fields are retained; source commit, original-input SHA-256 and acquisition date identify provenance. The figure shows the last twelve addition-month bins, including the partial current month. Counts describe catalog additions, not attacks, victim counts, exploitation onset or overall vulnerability prevalence. Unlisted CVEs are not negative labels. The publisher's [mirror and CC0 scope](https://github.com/cisagov/kev-data) support this metadata use.

# HELIOS graduate research protocol

A credible cyberengineering result connects mission consequence to a defensible mechanism, an observation model and an experiment that can fail. This extension preserves missions 001–150 and adds proposed missions 151–180. Six small executable reference models test mechanics; they do not implement the complete missions or establish field effectiveness. The new mathematics is an author-proposed research formulation, not a formula mandated by the cited standards.

## State the claim before selecting a tool

Specify the population, system boundary, intervention, comparator, endpoint and minimum meaningful effect. For a telemetry detector, an example endpoint is fewer false alerts per observed sensor-hour at a fixed event-recall floor. A latency endpoint must state whether time begins at event onset, first available observation or analyst receipt. For recovery, define lost service-minutes and finite staffing. For proofs, separate a reachable finite-state violation from an unbounded theorem and from implementation conformance.

| Record | Required content | Review question |
|---|---|---|
| Mission requirement | Essential function, owner, demand and consequence | Which decision changes if the research succeeds? |
| Threat and fault model | Allowed actor capabilities abstractly; benign faults, environmental conditions and trust assumptions | Could a benign process produce the same observation? |
| Observation model | Sensor coverage, timestamps, sampling, missingness and label source | What cannot be inferred from absence? |
| Mechanism | Variables, units, state transitions, interfaces and objective | Does the implementation actually test this mechanism? |
| Comparator | Operational practice and simple credible baseline | Are information, compute and tuning budgets equal? |
| Falsifier | Result that rejects the thesis | Is failure reported as openly as success? |
| Resource contract | RAM, storage, analyst-hours, energy and external dependencies | Is the proposed system feasible under actual constraints? |

## Statistical design

Split by time, host/channel, artifact family, team or failure scenario as appropriate. Never randomly split overlapping windows and then describe the test set as independent. Keep transformation fitting, hyperparameter selection and threshold selection inside training/validation. Predeclare a final untouched test partition and record every reuse. In rare-event detection, report prevalence, precision, recall, false-positive rate and alert burden together; high accuracy can reflect always predicting the majority class.

For Bernoulli outcomes, justify sample size from the intended interval width or detectable effect, then adjust for correlated units and event scarcity. A rough independent-event planning relation is $n \approx z_{0.975}^2 p(1-p)/h^2$, where $h$ is the desired half-width; it is not adequate for clustered telemetry or sparse zero-error results. Zero failures does not demonstrate zero risk: the independent-trial upper-bound heuristic is approximately $3/n$ at 95%, and dependence makes effective $n$ smaller. Use scenario/team/channel-level resampling when observations share causes. The included 50-row block bootstrap is an illustrative finite-fixture diagnostic; justify block duration from the correlation structure for real data.

Paired interventions on the same scenarios reduce nuisance variation. Report effect size with uncertainty and a resource-normalized comparator, not a p-value alone. For 180 proposals, do not interpret many exploratory significant results as 180 confirmations: preregister confirmatory endpoints, label exploratory analyses and choose a multiplicity strategy before inspecting the outcomes. A non-significant result does not establish equivalence; an equivalence claim requires a prespecified acceptable difference and suitable test.

## Identification and causal interpretation

A useful causal study distinguishes intervention selection, observation availability and the outcome. This proposed diagram makes a common failure visible:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U["Baseline mission risk"] --> I["Control investment"]
  U --> Y["Mission loss"]
  I --> Y
  I --> O["Observation coverage"]
  O --> R["Recorded incidents"]
  Y --> R
```

Recorded incidents may increase when observation improves even while mission loss decreases. A before/after plot alone cannot distinguish that effect. Write the adjustment set and justify overlap, intervention consistency, interference and the missingness mechanism. If assumptions cannot be defended, provide sensitivity bounds or descriptive associations. A detector disagreement, physical residual or catalog membership is not causal attribution of malicious behavior.

## Graduate challenges that deserve experiments

1. **Partial observability:** distinguish unknown state from favorable state; explicitly model missed sensors and incomplete labels.
2. **Nonstationarity:** hold out operating modes, calendar periods and device families; evaluate adaptation against a frozen baseline without learning from future labels.
3. **Compositional assurance:** connect a proof, build digest and hardware/environment assumption to the same evaluated revision; one valid component does not establish system validity.
4. **Common causes:** model shared power, keys, clocks, suppliers and operator availability. Multiplying component availability assumes independence that often needs evidence.
5. **Identifiability:** determine which parameters can be learned from the chosen observations before optimizing them. Strong regularization cannot manufacture missing information.
6. **Tail risk:** compare mean loss and a declared tail metric; uncertain heavy-tailed restore times can reverse a seemingly optimal schedule.
7. **Human coupling:** workload, accessibility, handoffs and incentives affect measured outcomes. Use consent, blinded grading and team-level dependence in human studies.
8. **External validity:** compare source and target environments explicitly. Historical telemetry and laboratory fixtures do not establish contemporary deployment performance.

## Delivery gates

| Gate | Reviewable artifact | Exit criterion |
|---|---|---|
| G0 concept | Thesis, scope, source ledger, rival mechanism | Distinct scientific question and observable endpoint |
| G1 formalization | State/schema, units, assumptions, identifiability analysis | An independent reviewer can reconstruct the claim |
| G2 reference model | Fixture, baseline, adverse cases and deterministic outputs | Known analytical or fixture truth checks pass |
| G3 benchmark | Pinned lawful data, untouched partition, uncertainty and ablations | Results survive declared comparisons and negative controls |
| G4 isolated pilot | Resource use, task success, rollback and owner approval | All local safety/privacy/availability requirements hold |
| G5 operational study | Monitored deployment and independent review | Evidence supports the narrow stated population and conditions |

This change reaches G2 for six mechanics only. The individual missions remain G0–G1 proposals. Dataset acquisition beyond the KEV metadata snapshot, complete systems, independent scientific review, human studies and operational pilots remain future work.

## Reading path and source roles

[NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Rev. 1](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/160/v2/r1/final) grounds resilience objectives and systems-engineering context. [NASA-STD-8739.8B](https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/nasa/nasa-std-87398) grounds software assurance, safety and independent verification responsibilities. [NIST SP 800-226](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/226/final) grounds evaluation of differential-privacy claims. These sources guide design review; they do not validate the proposed algorithms, provide cyber-event frequencies or endorse HELIOS.

# Applicable datasets and engineering resources

Reviewed 2026-10-02. Only the filtered, version-pinned KEV metadata was acquired from an external source. Six local benchmark fixtures are generated synthetically. Other entries are acquisition plans or design resources, not downloaded or validated training datasets.

[Machine-readable ledger](../data/research/resources.json) · [KEV snapshot](../data/research/kev_snapshot.json) · [Protocol](METHOD.md)

## LANL · LANL Comprehensive Multi-Source Cyber-Security Events

[Primary resource](https://csr.lanl.gov/data/cyber1/)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Observed enterprise event data; access form; not downloaded.
**Applicable question:** Authentication/process/DNS/flow correlation and missing-observation studies.
**Fields:** De-identified identifiers, relative seconds, authentication outcomes and flows.
**Evaluation hazards:** Split chronologically and by entity; the small red-team label set is incomplete; absence of a label is not a negative truth. Failed-auth inclusion is conditional on at least one successful auth.
**Resources:** 58 days, approximately 12 GB compressed; plan streaming aggregation rather than full RAM loading.
**Rights:** CC0 waiver stated by publisher; human-subject and public-release approvals documented.
**Inspection:** landing page and schema inspected.

## TELEMANOM · Telemanom SMAP/MSL anomaly data and original study

[Primary resource](https://github.com/khundman/telemanom)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Public telemetry benchmark; not downloaded.
**Applicable question:** Spacecraft anomaly detection; benign operational anomalies do not label cyber compromise.
**Fields:** Channel arrays and labeled anomaly intervals; inspect README preprocessing before use.
**Evaluation hazards:** Hold out channels/time; avoid random overlapping window splits and inflated point-adjusted recall; report per-event as well as per-timestamp scoring.
**Resources:** Array data and Python ecosystem; size and dependencies must be checked at pinned revision.
**Rights:** Repository license and dataset terms require review before redistribution.
**Inspection:** author repository inspected; NASA paper https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20210008188.

## KEV · CISA KEV issuer-maintained data mirror

[Primary resource](https://github.com/cisagov/kev-data)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Observed public catalog metadata; 1731 selected records downloaded.
**Applicable question:** Descriptive catalog timing and owned-inventory relevance.
**Fields:** CVE identifier, vendor, product, addition date, ransomware-use indicator.
**Evaluation hazards:** Snapshot SHA and date; addition date is not exploitation onset; missing KEV membership does not mean unexploited. No exploit descriptions or target records are included.
**Resources:** Small JSON metadata; offline processing.
**Rights:** CC0 per issuer README and LICENSE.
**Inspection:** repository and license inspected; pinned source commit in kev_snapshot.json.

## BORG · Google Borg cluster and power traces

[Primary resource](https://github.com/google/cluster-data)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Observed workload/power resource; not downloaded.
**Applicable question:** Cloud scheduling, resource-budget and correlated workload sensitivity.
**Fields:** Task and machine events, usage; 2019 power trace is separately documented.
**Evaluation hazards:** Temporal and cell holdouts; workload failures are not attacks; job identities and workload mix may not transfer to another environment.
**Resources:** Potentially large trace/query workflow; choose fields and downsample with declared policy.
**Rights:** CC-BY per publisher; retain attribution and inspect exact license.
**Inspection:** publisher repository inspected.

## CFREDS · NIST Computer Forensic Reference Data Sets

[Primary resource](https://cfreds.nist.gov/)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Forensic reference fixtures; not downloaded.
**Applicable question:** Known-ground-truth acquisition/parser and inference evaluation.
**Fields:** Fixture-specific artifacts, hashes, descriptions and truth labels.
**Evaluation hazards:** Pin fixture and documented truth; tool behavior on one fixture does not establish evidentiary validity in all cases.
**Resources:** Fixture-specific storage and read-only tooling.
**Rights:** Review each dataset terms; portal license is not automatically fixture license.
**Inspection:** portal resolved but text not retrievable; fixture contents unverified.

## TLA · TLA+ specification examples

[Primary resource](https://github.com/tlaplus/Examples)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Formal specifications/tool examples; not empirical field data.
**Applicable question:** Revocation, concurrency, refinement and proof-assumption studies.
**Fields:** Specification, configuration, invariants and state bounds.
**Evaluation hazards:** Document abstraction and fairness; finite model checking is not an unbounded proof; use a separate implementation trace refinement check.
**Resources:** TLC/Java or equivalent; state space can dominate RAM.
**Rights:** Inspect per-project licensing before reuse.
**Inspection:** maintainer repository inspected.

## OPENTITAN · OpenTitan device life-cycle specification

[Primary resource](https://opentitan.org/book/doc/security/specs/device_life_cycle/)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Hardware design resource; not measured board data.
**Applicable question:** Firmware recovery and device-state trust review.
**Fields:** Declared device states, transition permissions, implementation constraints.
**Evaluation hazards:** Project-specific architecture; does not validate a derivative device or certify physical fault resistance.
**Resources:** Emulator first; optional owned low-voltage dev board, qualified hardware review.
**Rights:** Documentation/source terms require review before copying implementation.
**Inspection:** primary device-lifecycle documentation inspected.

## SLSA · SLSA specification v1.2

[Primary resource](https://slsa.dev/spec/v1.2/)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Versioned provenance requirements; not a labeled dataset.
**Applicable question:** Artifact identity, source/build provenance and freshness study.
**Fields:** Provenance predicate, subject digests, builder and source identity.
**Evaluation hazards:** Evidence validity differs from software correctness; a claimed level requires all actual evidence requirements.
**Resources:** Owned build artifacts, local verifier, snapshot statements.
**Rights:** Follow specification/documentation license and upstream verifier license.
**Inspection:** v1.2 primary specification inspected.

## CFS · NASA Core Flight System

[Primary resource](https://github.com/nasa/cFS)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Flight-software architecture resource; not live mission command access.
**Applicable question:** Offline remote-operation state models and assurance traceability.
**Fields:** Framework interfaces, tests, versioned build and configuration.
**Evaluation hazards:** Do not infer flight readiness or certification from source availability; study command handling and scheduling in an emulator.
**Resources:** Pinned framework checkout and toolchain; submodules separately pinned.
**Rights:** Check each component license and export/distribution notes.
**Inspection:** NASA-maintained repository inspected.

## OTEL · OpenTelemetry documentation

[Primary resource](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Instrumentation schemas/tooling; no third-party telemetry downloaded.
**Applicable question:** Owned-system trace, metric and log correlation.
**Fields:** Trace IDs, spans, event time, service/resource attributes and collection loss.
**Evaluation hazards:** Sampling and asynchronous export create partial observation; exclude secrets and personal attributes from synthetic fixtures.
**Resources:** Optional owned collector and local workload; benchmark supplied here is offline.
**Rights:** Review implementation license and data handling separately.
**Inspection:** primary documentation inspected.

## SYNTHETIC · HELIOS deterministic local fixtures

[Primary resource](../experiments/benchmark.py)

**Evidence and acquisition:** Synthetic; generated locally with declared seed 20261002.
**Applicable question:** Reproducible model mechanics and failure-case evaluation.
**Fields:** Six benchmark fixtures, model assumptions, summary, output hashes.
**Evaluation hazards:** Demonstrates reference algorithms only; neither population realism nor deployed defensive effectiveness follows.
**Resources:** Python standard library; no network or cloud services.
**Rights:** New author-generated fixture data; no imported private telemetry.
**Inspection:** implemented and tested in this change.

## Acquisition record

For any future imported dataset, retain the exact URL/DOI, immutable revision or object ID, source hash, UTC acquisition time, declared rights, collection window, schema, units, missingness and label semantics. Never submit contact information or agree to additional terms merely to complete this ledger. Respect gated access; use a documented synthetic fixture while data access is pending.

The KEV projection keeps five metadata fields and deliberately excludes descriptions, remediation prose and external links. Its source SHA-256 binds the full upstream input; the retained subset has its own repository identity. Descriptive aggregates count catalog entries and addition dates, not attacks or exploitation rates.

# Validation and remaining research

Prepared against repository revision `a9fc2a752620ba211bd6ca04cf8bb03da4f679db` on 2026-10-02. This record describes reproducible local checks. The [Atlas integrity workflow history](https://github.com/Personfu/CyberEngineering/actions/workflows/atlas.yml) provides the separate remote validation record for each published commit.

- The separate extension catalog includes missions 001–180 exactly once, with 30 unique additions and 180 individual research dossiers.

- Twenty-six unit/integrity tests cover missing-observation semantics, threshold partitioning, fixture truth, recovery prerequisites/objective, update interruption boundaries, temporal ambiguity, privacy parameters, contact receipts, metadata provenance and preservation.

The 30 new missions and deeper 150 dossiers remain research proposals. Six bounded mechanics have local fixture validation only. Only the five-field, 1,731-record CISA metadata projection was acquired externally.
